note:
Hospital day 3 endocrinology follow-up progress note.

This is a 53-year-old male admitted three days ago with dehydration, acute kidney injury, and alcohol withdrawal after returning from a two-week trip to Southeast Asia, where he had several days of watery diarrhea. A non-contrast CT chest obtained on admission for a persistent cough incidentally showed a right thyroid nodule, and we were asked to evaluate it. His past medical history includes T2DM, HTN, hyperlipidemia, GERD, and alcohol use disorder. He reports drinking eight to ten beers daily for several years, with his last drink the day before admission.

Interval events: No seizures or hallucinations overnight. CIWA scores have been 3 to 5 and he needed lorazepam 1 mg PRN only once in the last 24 hours. The diarrhea has resolved and stool studies were negative. He reports the cough is improving.

Thyroid history: He had not noticed a neck lump before this admission. He denies neck pain, dysphagia, hoarseness, shortness of breath, palpitations, heat intolerance, and weight loss. He has had no prior neck radiation and no family history of thyroid cancer. He has not taken iodine or biotin supplements.

Medication reconciliation was clarified today. He first told us he takes metformin 500 mg twice daily, but the outpatient pharmacy fill history shows 1000 mg twice daily, and he confirmed this after reading the bottle with his wife by phone. Correction, the home dose is metformin 1000 mg twice daily. Metformin has been held since admission because of the AKI and alcohol use. Lisinopril 20 mg daily was also stopped on admission for the AKI. Current inpatient medications are amlodipine, increased from 5 mg to 10 mg daily yesterday for elevated BP, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, pantoprazole 40 mg daily, thiamine 100 mg daily, folic acid 1 mg daily, insulin lispro sliding scale with meals, and lorazepam 1 mg PRN per the CIWA protocol. No known drug allergies.

Vitals this morning: temp 98.6 F, BP 148/88, HR 88, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air.

Exam: He is alert, in no distress, and has no tremor at rest. Thyroid exam shows a firm, nontender, 2 cm nodule in the right lobe that moves with swallowing; the left lobe is normal to palpation. No cervical lymphadenopathy, no tracheal deviation, no exophthalmos, and no lid lag. Lungs are clear. Abdomen is soft and nontender.

Data: Na 137, K 3.9, creatinine 1.2 (peak 1.9 on admission), glucose 142, WBC 7.4, Hgb 13.1, platelets 118, INR 1.2. AST 88, ALT 46. TSH 1.1 and free T4 1.2 are both normal. HbA1c 7.8%. Calcium 9.3. Thyroid ultrasound shows a 2.1 cm solid hypoechoic nodule in the right lower pole with microcalcifications and a taller-than-wide shape, ACR TI-RADS 5; the left lobe is normal and there are no abnormal cervical lymph nodes. Non-contrast CT chest shows no pulmonary mass or consolidation and no mediastinal extension of the nodule.

Assessment and plan:
1. Right thyroid nodule, 2.1 cm, ACR TI-RADS 5 with highly suspicious sonographic features, in a clinically and biochemically euthyroid patient. Plan ultrasound-guided FNA of the right thyroid nodule tomorrow morning before discharge; INR and platelets are acceptable for the procedure. Send calcitonin with morning labs. No thyroid scan or radioactive iodine is indicated with a normal TSH.
2. Alcohol withdrawal, improving. Continue thiamine, folic acid, and lorazepam PRN per CIWA. Addiction medicine consult requested for alcohol use disorder.
3. AKI, resolving. Continue to hold metformin and lisinopril until creatinine is stable at baseline and he is abstinent. Continue amlodipine 10 mg daily.
4. T2DM with HbA1c 7.8%. Insulin sliding scale in house; resume metformin 1000 mg twice daily at discharge if renal function allows.
5. Follow up in endocrinology clinic in two weeks to review cytology; surgical referral if the result is suspicious or malignant. He verbalized understanding of the plan.
summary: A 53-year-old male with T2DM, HTN, and alcohol use disorder, hospitalized with dehydration, acute kidney injury, and alcohol withdrawal after travel to Southeast Asia, was evaluated on hospital day 3 for a right thyroid nodule found incidentally on CT chest. He is euthyroid with a normal TSH and has no compressive symptoms. Thyroid ultrasound shows a 2.1 cm solid hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications, ACR TI-RADS 5. The plan is ultrasound-guided FNA before discharge, calcitonin, continued withdrawal management, and holding metformin and lisinopril while the AKI resolves, with amlodipine raised to 10 mg daily. Endocrinology follow-up in two weeks will review cytology.

note: Dermatology clinic dictation. This is a 50-year-old female seen for a changing pigmented lesion on her upper back. She noticed it about four months ago, and her husband says it has grown and become darker over that time. She denies itching, bleeding, or pain from the lesion, and she denies any ulceration or crusting. She has never had a skin cancer or an atypical mole removed before. She reports several blistering sunburns as a teenager and does not use tanning beds. Past medical history is significant for hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 75 mcg daily. No known drug allergies. On exam, there is a pigmented macule on the left upper back measuring about six millimeters, correction, seven millimeters, with asymmetry, an irregular border, and variegated brown and black color. Dermoscopy shows an atypical network with focal blue-gray areas. No other suspicious lesions were seen on full skin examination, and there is no palpable cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. Impression is an atypical pigmented lesion, suspicious for dysplastic nevus versus early melanoma. Plan is a complete excisional biopsy today with two millimeter margins under local lidocaine 1 percent with epinephrine, sent to dermatopathology. Wound care instructions given: keep it dry for 24 hours, then use petroleum jelly and a bandage, and sutures out in two weeks when we will review the pathology result. She was advised on daily sunscreen and sun protection and monthly self skin checks. Continue levothyroxine. End of dictation.

She denies itching, bleeding, pain, ulceration, and crusting. The seven millimeter left upper back macule is asymmetric with an irregular border and variegated color, and dermoscopy shows an atypical network with focal blue-gray areas, with no lymphadenopathy. The impression is an atypical pigmented lesion suspicious for dysplastic nevus versus early melanoma. A complete excisional biopsy with two millimeter margins was planned today under local lidocaine, with pathology review and suture removal in two weeks, and sun protection counseling was given.

note: Psychiatry consultation dictation on the medical floor. The patient is a 44-year-old male admitted overnight with chest pain who has now been medically cleared, with two negative troponins, a normal EKG, and a normal TSH. He describes three months of recurrent attacks of sudden pounding heart, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, and a feeling that he is going to die. The attacks peak within ten minutes, last about twenty minutes, and occur two to three times per week. Between attacks he worries constantly about the next one and has started avoiding driving alone, correction, avoiding driving on the highway alone. He denies suicidal ideation, denies homicidal ideation, denies hallucinations, and denies alcohol or drug use. He drinks one cup of coffee a day. He has no prior psychiatric treatment, no medical problems, and takes no medications. On mental status exam he is anxious but cooperative, speech is normal in rate and rhythm, thought process is linear, mood is nervous, affect is congruent, there is no evidence of psychosis, and insight is good. Impression is panic disorder. Plan is to start sertraline 25 mg daily for one week and then increase to 50 mg daily, avoid benzodiazepines, refer for cognitive behavioral therapy, follow up with outpatient psychiatry in two weeks, and give him education about panic attacks with reassurance that his cardiac work-up was normal. He is cleared for discharge from a psychiatric standpoint. End of dictation.

note:
Telehealth visit conducted as an audio-only telephone call, with a professional Vietnamese medical interpreter on the line throughout. The patient is at home with his daughter present, and verbal consent for the telephone visit was obtained. This is a 94-year-old male seen for follow-up of mild cognitive impairment and poor sleep.

History: The daughter reports that over the past year he has been forgetting appointments and repeating questions, and he sometimes misplaces his keys and glasses. He still dresses, bathes, and feeds himself independently, while she manages his pills and finances. She denies falls, hallucinations, getting lost outside, or new confusion. The patient himself denies low mood, headaches, and weakness on one side. He takes diphenhydramine 25 mg nightly from the pharmacy shelf to help him sleep and says he feels groggy in the mornings. He has not driven for several years.

Past medical history: hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hearing loss. Current medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, aspirin 81 mg daily, and diphenhydramine as above. No known drug allergies.

Home measurements: The daughter checked his blood pressure with a home cuff just before the call and it was 128/72 with a pulse of 64.

Limited exam by phone: Speech is fluent and appropriate through the interpreter, he follows multi-step questions, and he was oriented to person, place, and the month but not the exact day. He recalled 2 of 3 words at five minutes. No visual exam was possible.

Data reviewed: CT head six months ago showed mild age-related atrophy and chronic small vessel changes without mass or infarct. B12 was 540 and TSH was 2.1 on the last labs.

Impression: Mild cognitive impairment, stable, with likely contribution from nightly anticholinergic use and hearing loss. Hypertension appears controlled based on the home reading.

Next steps: Stop diphenhydramine today. Start melatonin 3 mg at bedtime. Continue amlodipine, atorvastatin, and aspirin at current doses. Refer for a hearing evaluation. Repeat in-person cognitive testing with MoCA in 3 months. The daughter will keep using the pill organizer and supervise medications. Sleep hygiene was reviewed through the interpreter, and the patient and daughter verbalized understanding. Call sooner for sudden confusion, falls, or new hallucinations. Follow up in person in 3 months.

Over the past year he has been forgetting appointments and repeating questions, while remaining independent in basic self-care, and he feels groggy in the mornings after taking diphenhydramine nightly for sleep. A home blood pressure was 128/72, and phone screening showed recall of 2 of 3 words. The assessment is stable mild cognitive impairment with contributions from anticholinergic use and hearing loss. Diphenhydramine is stopped and melatonin started, a hearing evaluation is arranged, and in-person MoCA testing is planned in 3 months.

Nurse: This is an 85-year-old female here with right flank pain that started about two hours ago. She was in the hospital about three weeks ago. Vitals are BP 154/82, heart rate 96, temp 98.6, and 97% on room air.

Doctor: Hello, I'm the emergency doctor. Tell me what's going on.

Patient: Oh, it's the worst pain. Right here in my back, going down toward my groin. It comes in waves and I can't get comfortable.

Doctor: When did it start?

Patient: About two hours ago, I was just sitting watching TV. I threw up once too.

Doctor: Any fever or chills?

Patient: No fever, no chills.

Doctor: Any burning when you pee?

Patient: No burning. But my urine looked pinkish this morning.

Doctor: Have you ever had a kidney stone before?

Patient: Never.

Doctor: You were in the hospital recently. What was that for?

Patient: Pneumonia, three weeks ago. I was there five days and they sent me home on antibiotics, which I finished. Since I got home I've been taking ibuprofen for my knees, 400 milligrams two or three times a day.

Doctor: Okay, that's good to know. Any belly pain, diarrhea, chest pain, or trouble breathing?

Patient: No belly pain, no diarrhea. No chest pain, no trouble breathing. The cough is almost gone.

Doctor: What other medicines do you take?

Patient: Amlodipine 5 milligrams every morning. That's all, besides the ibuprofen.

Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?

Patient: No, none.

Doctor: Okay. Let me examine you. Your belly is soft and not tender, but you're quite tender when I tap on your right back over the kidney. Heart sounds regular, lungs clear, and your legs aren't swollen.

Doctor: Your results are back. Your urine test shows a lot of blood but no sign of infection. Your white count is 9.8, and your creatinine, which is your kidney function, is 1.3. That is a little higher than the 1.0 you had when you left the hospital. The CT scan shows a 5 millimeter stone in the right ureter, the tube from the kidney to the bladder, with mild hydronephrosis, which means some swelling of the kidney behind the stone.

Patient: Oh no. What do we do?

Doctor: This is renal colic from a kidney stone. Many stones this size pass on their own. We gave you acetaminophen 1000 milligrams through the IV and ondansetron 4 milligrams for the nausea, and I see your pain is better now. Because of your age and your kidney numbers, I want you to stop the ibuprofen. It can hurt the kidneys. For pain at home, take acetaminophen 650 milligrams every 6 hours as needed, and I'm giving you a small supply of oxycodone 2.5 milligrams every 6 hours as needed for severe pain only, 8 tablets. It can make you sleepy and constipated, so be careful when you stand up. Drink plenty of fluids and strain your urine. See urology in about one week, and have your kidney function rechecked with your regular doctor in a few days. Come back right away for fever, uncontrolled pain, vomiting you can't stop, or if you can't pee.

Patient: Okay, I understand.
summary: An 85-year-old female hospitalized for pneumonia three weeks ago presented with two hours of severe right flank pain radiating toward the groin, one episode of vomiting, and pink-tinged urine, without fever, chills, or burning. She had been taking ibuprofen for knee pain since discharge. Exam showed right costovertebral tenderness, urine with blood but no infection, a creatinine of 1.3, and a 5 millimeter right ureteral stone with mild hydronephrosis on CT. The diagnosis is renal colic from a kidney stone. Ibuprofen is stopped, acetaminophen and a small supply of oxycodone are given for pain, and she will see urology in about a week.

note:
Nurse: This is a 17-year-old female here for facial redness and bumps. Vitals: BP 108/64, heart rate 72, temp 98.2.

Doctor: Hi there. What's been going on with your face?

Patient: My cheeks and nose have been red for like four months. They get really hot and flushed, especially after I eat spicy food or when I'm out in the sun. And I've got these little bumps.

Doctor: Any burning or stinging?

Patient: Yeah, it stings when I put moisturizer on.

Doctor: Any blackheads?

Patient: No, not really. My friends have acne but mine doesn't look like that.

Doctor: Any eye problems, like dryness or a gritty feeling?

Patient: No, my eyes are fine.

Doctor: Any joint pain, rashes on other parts of your body, or fever?

Patient: No, nothing like that.

Doctor: What have you tried so far?

Patient: A hydrocortisone cream from the pharmacy, 1 percent, about twice a day for two weeks. It helped for a day and then it looked worse.

Doctor: Okay. Are you taking any vitamins or supplements?

Patient: I take niacin, 500 milligrams every day, because I read it's good for energy and hair. And biotin gummies, 5000 micrograms daily.

Doctor: That's helpful. Any medical conditions or allergies?

Patient: No. No allergies.

Doctor: Alright. On exam, there's redness over the cheeks, nose, and chin, with a few small red bumps and a couple of pustules. I can see fine visible blood vessels on the cheeks. No blackheads. Your eyelids look normal. I also did a quick skin scraping from the cheek and looked at it under the microscope with a KOH prep, and it was negative for fungus and no mites were seen.

Patient: So what is it?

Doctor: This looks like rosacea. The flushing is probably being made worse by the niacin, and steroid creams can make rosacea worse too. So I'd like you to stop the hydrocortisone cream and stop the niacin. I'd also stop the biotin, since it can cause breakouts. For treatment, start metronidazole 0.75 percent gel once a day on the whole face after washing, use a gentle moisturizer, and a mineral sunscreen with SPF 30 every morning. Try to avoid triggers like spicy food, hot drinks, and a lot of sun. It takes six to eight weeks to see improvement, so be patient.

Patient: Is it going to go away?

Doctor: It's a chronic condition, but we can control it well. Follow up with a dermatologist in six weeks, and if it's not better we can add other treatments. Come back sooner if your eyes become red or painful, or the redness spreads.

Patient: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 17-year-old female presented to urgent care with four months of facial redness, flushing triggered by spicy food and sun, small bumps, and stinging with moisturizer. She denies blackheads, eye problems, joint pain, rashes elsewhere, and fever, and she had tried hydrocortisone cream, which made it look worse. She also takes over-the-counter niacin and biotin. Exam showed redness with papules, pustules, and visible blood vessels, and a KOH prep was negative for fungus with no mites seen. The diagnosis is rosacea, so hydrocortisone cream, niacin, and biotin are stopped, metronidazole gel is started, and dermatology follow-up is set for six weeks.

note: Orthopedic surgery inpatient progress dictation, postoperative day 2 following right total hip arthroplasty. This is an 84-year-old female who underwent a right total hip arthroplasty through a posterior approach for end-stage osteoarthritis. She had no events overnight. She reports her pain is 4 out of 10 at rest and 6 out of 10 with physical therapy, controlled on acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours scheduled and oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed, which replaced the IV hydromorphone yesterday. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, calf pain, and numbness or tingling in the right foot. She has mild constipation with no bowel movement since surgery. She still works part-time overnight shifts as a home health aide, so her sleep schedule is irregular and she sleeps mostly during the day. Vitals this morning: temperature 99.0 F, heart rate 82, blood pressure 126/70, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. On exam she is alert and comfortable. The incision is clean, dry, and intact with no erythema or drainage. The right leg is neurovascularly intact with intact pedal pulses, no calf tenderness, and no swelling beyond what is expected. Hemoglobin this morning is 9.8, correction, 9.6, down from 12.1 before surgery. Creatinine is 0.9. Postoperative AP pelvis and lateral right hip x-rays show the components in good position without fracture or dislocation. Assessment is postoperative day 2 status post right total hip arthroplasty, doing well, with mild acute blood loss anemia that is stable and mild constipation. Plan: continue physical therapy and occupational therapy with weight bearing as tolerated using a walker and posterior hip precautions for six weeks. Continue acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours scheduled and oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed. Start docusate 100 mg twice daily for constipation. Continue enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily in the hospital, and at discharge switch to aspirin 81 mg twice daily for four weeks for clot prevention. Because of her shift work, I asked nursing to time the scheduled doses to her actual sleep-wake pattern, and she will use a pill organizer with phone alarms at home. She should not return to work for six weeks, and a work note was provided. Discharge home with home health physical therapy tomorrow if she meets therapy goals, with clinic follow-up in two weeks for a wound check. End of dictation.

note:
Nurse: This is a 61-year-old male here for follow-up of a blood clot in his left leg. He was in the hospital about three weeks ago. Vitals today are BP 134/80, heart rate 76, temp 98.1, and 98% on room air.

Doctor: Good to see you. How's the leg doing?

Patient: Better, honestly. The swelling has gone down a lot and the calf doesn't hurt like it did. It's still a little tight when I walk a long way.

Doctor: Remind me what happened.

Patient: I had my colon surgery for diverticulitis about three weeks ago, and I was in the hospital for six days. Then about eight days ago my left leg blew up, swollen, red, and sore. They did an ultrasound and found a clot.

Doctor: Right, the Doppler showed a clot in the left femoral and popliteal veins, and you've been on apixaban since then.

Patient: Yes, I took 10 milligrams twice a day for the first week. I finished that yesterday.

Doctor: Good. Any bleeding at all? Black stools, blood in your urine, nosebleeds, or bleeding gums?

Patient: No, none of that. No bruising either.

Doctor: Any chest pain, trouble breathing, or coughing up blood?

Patient: No, nothing like that.

Doctor: What other medications are you on?

Patient: Lisinopril 10 milligrams in the morning for my blood pressure, atorvastatin 20 milligrams at night, and Tylenol once in a while for the soreness.

Doctor: Any ibuprofen, Advil, or Aleve?

Patient: No, I've been avoiding those since the surgeon told me.

Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?

Patient: None.

Doctor: Anyone in your family had blood clots?

Patient: No.

Doctor: Okay, let me look at the leg. Your left calf measures about one centimeter bigger than the right, there's mild tenderness in the calf, but no redness and no warmth. The pulses in your foot are good. Your heart is regular and your lungs are clear. Your labs from today look fine too: hemoglobin is 13.4, platelets are 245, and your creatinine is 1.0.

Patient: So what does that mean?

Doctor: This is a provoked DVT, a clot that formed because of the surgery and being in the hospital, and it's improving. Now that you finished the first week, drop the apixaban from 10 milligrams to 5 milligrams twice a day, starting today. We'll keep you on it for three months total, and then reassess. Since there's a clear trigger, you don't need extensive clotting tests. Keep walking, avoid long periods of sitting, and keep avoiding ibuprofen and Aleve, though Tylenol is fine. Go to the ER right away for chest pain, trouble breathing, coughing up blood, or any bleeding that doesn't stop. I'll see you back here in three months.

Patient: Okay, that makes sense.
summary: A 61-year-old male seen in hematology clinic for follow-up of a left leg blood clot diagnosed about eight days ago, after colon surgery for diverticulitis and a six-day hospital stay three weeks ago. His swelling and calf pain have improved, and he denies black stools, blood in the urine, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, bruising, chest pain, trouble breathing, and coughing up blood. The left calf is a centimeter larger than the right with mild tenderness, and his hemoglobin, platelets, and creatinine are normal. The impression is a provoked DVT that is improving. Apixaban is reduced from 10 milligrams to 5 milligrams twice a day for three months total, with follow-up in three months.

note:
Hospital day 3 progress note for a 64-year-old female admitted with acute decompensated heart failure.

Interval events: There were no rapid response calls and no arrhythmia on telemetry overnight. She slept propped up on two pillows, down from three pillows at home, and says her breathing is better but she is still short of breath when walking to the bathroom. She was anxious this morning and asked many questions, including whether she will need a pacemaker, why her weight matters so much, and whether she can ever eat out again. Each question was answered and we reviewed the plan together. Her daughter, who lives with her and is her main caregiver, was at the bedside and provided part of the history. The daughter reports that over the past week the patient gained about 8 pounds, had worsening leg swelling, woke at night gasping for air, and was taking over-the-counter ibuprofen for knee pain up to three times daily. The patient denies chest pain, fever, productive cough, palpitations, and syncope.

Past medical history: HFrEF due to ischemic cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, CKD stage 3, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. No known drug allergies.

Medication reconciliation was clarified today. The daughter first said the patient takes carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, but when she brought in the pill bottles the label read 12.5 mg twice daily, so the correct home dose is carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily. Other home medications are spironolactone 25 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and metformin 500 mg twice daily. In the hospital, furosemide IV was increased this morning from 40 mg to 80 mg twice daily because she was net negative only 600 mL over the last 24 hours. Carvedilol, spironolactone, apixaban, and atorvastatin are continued. Ibuprofen has been discontinued and should not be restarted. Metformin is on hold, and she receives insulin lispro sliding scale. She was also given potassium chloride 40 mEq by mouth for hypokalemia.

Vitals this morning: temp 98.2 F, HR 78, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal cannula. Weight is 78.4 kg, down from 82.1 kg on admission.

Exam: She is anxious but comfortable at rest. JVP is elevated at about 10 cm, there are bibasilar crackles, and her rhythm is irregularly irregular with a 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex. She has 2+ pitting edema to the knees, her abdomen is soft, and her extremities are warm.

Data: BNP was 1450 on admission and troponin was negative twice. Today creatinine is 1.5 (baseline 1.3), K 3.4, Na 134, glucose 156, and Hgb 11.8. Chest X-ray shows pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions, improved from admission. Echo this admission showed an EF of 30%, down from 35% previously, with moderate mitral regurgitation. EKG shows atrial fibrillation with a controlled ventricular rate.

Assessment and plan:
1. Acute decompensated HFrEF, likely precipitated by NSAID use and dietary sodium. Continue furosemide 80 mg IV twice daily, daily weights, strict intake and output, a 2 g sodium diet, and fluid restriction of 1.5 L daily. Repeat BMP this afternoon. Expect to transition to an oral diuretic in 24 to 48 hours.
2. Mild creatinine rise above baseline, likely cardiorenal. Monitor with daily BMP and avoid nephrotoxins.
3. Hypokalemia. Potassium chloride given as above; recheck BMP this afternoon.
4. Atrial fibrillation, rate controlled. Continue carvedilol and apixaban at current doses.
5. Type 2 diabetes. Metformin held; continue sliding scale insulin.
6. Anxiety related to hospitalization. Reassurance given, questions answered, and written heart failure education provided to the patient and her daughter.
Disposition: Anticipate discharge in 3 to 4 days with heart failure clinic follow-up within 7 days of discharge and social work referral for a home scale.
summary: A 64-year-old female with HFrEF, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, and CKD stage 3 is on hospital day 3 for acute decompensated heart failure, likely triggered by ibuprofen use and dietary sodium. She remains short of breath walking, with bibasilar crackles, elevated JVP, and 2+ pitting edema, though weight is down from 82.1 to 78.4 kg and chest X-ray is improved. The carvedilol dose was corrected by pill bottle to 12.5 mg twice daily. Furosemide IV was increased to 80 mg twice daily, ibuprofen was discontinued, metformin is held, and potassium chloride was given for hypokalemia. Her anxiety was addressed with education, and discharge with heart failure clinic follow-up is planned.

The primary team asked us to see him because his admission labs showed an HbA1c of 5.9% and a fasting glucose of 112. He has no prior diagnosis of diabetes. He denies excessive thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, and unintentional weight loss. He reports gaining about 25 pounds over the last two years, drinks two to three sugar-sweetened sodas daily, and gets little exercise. He takes no regular medications. He is currently using acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for postoperative soreness. He has no known drug allergies.

Vitals today: BP 134/84, HR 76, RR 16, temp 98.6 F, SpO2 98% on room air. Weight is 104 kg with a BMI of 33 and a waist circumference of 108 cm. On exam he is comfortable, there is acanthosis nigricans on the posterior neck, and the laparoscopic port sites are clean, dry, and intact. Labs show HbA1c 5.9%, fasting glucose 112, triglycerides 190, HDL 36, LDL 118, creatinine 0.8, and a normal TSH of 1.9.

We will repeat HbA1c and a fasting lipid panel in three months and recheck his blood pressure at that visit. He will follow up in the endocrinology clinic in three months.
